# Project Proposal: Enterprise Deployment of an Internal AI Assistant

## Background

A 5,000-employee organization generates and relies on a substantial volume of information across policies, procedures, project documentation, business systems, and employee communications. Finding reliable answers often requires navigating multiple tools, searching disconnected repositories, or asking colleagues for help. These activities consume time, interrupt workflows, and create inconsistent access to organizational knowledge.

This project proposes deploying a secure internal AI assistant that helps employees find information, summarize approved content, draft routine materials, and complete selected workplace tasks. The assistant will serve as a common entry point to organizational knowledge while respecting existing access permissions and information security requirements. It will support employee judgment rather than replace it, with clear source references and safeguards for sensitive or consequential uses.

A phased deployment will allow the organization to validate value, establish governance, and address operational risks before extending access to all employees.

## Objectives

The primary objective is to reduce the time employees spend searching for information and completing repetitive knowledge-work tasks. The assistant will provide accessible, source-backed answers from approved internal resources and help employees prepare drafts, summaries, and other routine work products.

The project will also improve the consistency of internal information delivery, particularly for common questions about HR policies, IT services, organizational procedures, and onboarding. A further objective is to establish a reusable foundation for future AI capabilities, including governed integrations with business applications.

These outcomes will be pursued without weakening privacy, security, or accountability. Employees will retain responsibility for reviewing outputs, and the organization will maintain clear ownership of the assistant’s content, operation, and permitted uses.

## Scope

The initial deployment will provide a conversational assistant through an approved enterprise interface, integrated where practical with the organization’s existing collaboration environment. Employees will authenticate through single sign-on, and the assistant will retrieve information only from sources they are authorized to access.

The first release will cover approved HR policies, IT support documentation, onboarding materials, corporate procedures, and selected departmental knowledge repositories. Core capabilities will include answering questions with citations, summarizing accessible documents, drafting routine communications, and guiding employees through documented processes. Responses will distinguish retrieved organizational information from generated suggestions and acknowledge when available evidence is insufficient.

The project includes platform selection, security and privacy review, knowledge-source preparation, integration development, evaluation, employee training, support readiness, and adoption measurement. It also includes establishing policies for acceptable use, retention, audit logging, incident response, and ongoing content maintenance.

Autonomous execution of consequential actions will remain outside the initial scope. The assistant will not independently make employment decisions, authorize spending, alter access permissions, or provide binding legal, financial, or compliance determinations. Any later capability to submit requests or update business records will require a separate review, appropriate permissions, and explicit user confirmation.

## Delivery Timeline

The proposed delivery period is six months, followed by ongoing operation and improvement. The schedule assumes that procurement, identity integration, and access to priority knowledge sources can be completed without major delays.

During the first month, the project team will confirm priority use cases, establish baseline measures, assess candidate platforms, and define governance requirements. This phase will conclude with an approved solution design, a prioritized knowledge-source inventory, and an evaluation plan.

During months two and three, the team will configure the platform, implement authentication and permission-aware retrieval, connect initial repositories, and prepare content for reliable use. Testing will assess answer quality, citation accuracy, access controls, resilience, and resistance to malicious instructions embedded in retrieved content. A limited pilot of approximately 250 employees will begin once security and operational readiness criteria are met.

Month four will focus on evaluating the pilot and correcting deficiencies. Participants will represent different departments, roles, and working patterns. Their feedback, alongside measured task performance and support demand, will inform improvements to retrieval, user guidance, and training. Expansion will depend on meeting agreed quality and safety thresholds.

During months five and six, access will expand in controlled waves to approximately 1,000 employees and then to the full 5,000-employee organization. Each wave will include communications, role-relevant training, and support coverage. The deployment will conclude with a formal acceptance review and transition to a permanent service owner.

## Resource Requirements

The project will require an executive sponsor and a cross-functional delivery team. Core staffing should include a full-time project manager, a full-time product owner, two integration or platform engineers, one AI evaluation specialist, and one knowledge-management lead during implementation. Security, privacy, legal, procurement, identity management, accessibility, and IT operations teams will contribute at defined review points.

A change-management and training lead will coordinate launch communications, learning materials, and an employee champion network. Departmental content owners will validate authoritative sources, resolve conflicting guidance, and maintain materials after launch. Service desk staff will require training and clear escalation paths for technical issues, inaccurate responses, and suspected data exposure.

Technical resources will include an enterprise AI platform, a permission-aware retrieval service, approved model access, monitoring and evaluation tools, and separate development, test, and production environments. Vendor arrangements should address data handling, retention, subprocessors, service availability, and whether organizational data may be used for model training. Sensitive information will be minimized and handled according to organizational policy.

For planning purposes, the organization should reserve an indicative first-year budget of $1 million to $2 million, covering implementation effort, licensing or usage charges, integrations, security assurance, training, and support. This is a preliminary allowance rather than a vendor quote; the approved budget will depend on platform selection, usage patterns, existing contracts, and the extent to which internal staff can support delivery. Cost monitoring and usage controls will be established before broad rollout.

## Success Criteria

Success will be measured against baselines established during the first month. By the end of deployment, all eligible employees should have access, and at least 60 percent should have completed onboarding. Within three months of organization-wide launch, the target is for at least 50 percent of eligible employees to use the assistant monthly.

In controlled evaluations, users should complete selected information-finding and drafting tasks at least 20 percent faster than the baseline without a material reduction in work quality. At least 85 percent of evaluated responses should meet the agreed standard for correctness, relevance, and sufficient source support. Average user satisfaction should reach at least 4 out of 5 among surveyed active users.

Security acceptance will require no unresolved critical or high-severity findings at launch and successful permission-isolation testing across representative roles and repositories. The assistant must avoid presenting unsupported answers as verified organizational guidance and must direct users to authoritative sources or human support when needed.

Operational targets will include 99.5 percent monthly availability, excluding approved maintenance, and defined response and resolution times for incidents. Financial performance will be assessed through cost per active user, cost per interaction, and validated time savings. Results will be reported to the executive sponsor quarterly, with continued investment contingent on demonstrated value and acceptable risk.

## Governance and Long-Term Ownership

A steering group comprising business, technology, security, privacy, and employee-experience representatives will oversee deployment and approve material scope changes. After launch, a designated product owner and IT service owner will manage the assistant jointly, supported by departmental knowledge owners.

Ongoing operation will include regular quality evaluations, access-control checks, content reviews, and analysis of user feedback. Material changes to models, integrations, or retrieval behavior will be tested before release. Employees will receive clear guidance on appropriate use, verification of outputs, prohibited data handling, and reporting concerns.

Approval of this proposal will authorize a six-month, phased implementation and the initial discovery and design work. Funding and organization-wide rollout will proceed through defined decision gates, ensuring that the assistant is expanded only when its usefulness, security, and operational readiness have been demonstrated.

# Project Proposal: Deployment of an Internal AI Assistant

## Background

A 5,000-employee organization has a significant opportunity to improve how employees find information, complete routine work, and collaborate across departments. Internal knowledge is often distributed across document repositories, intranet pages, business applications, and individual teams. As a result, employees spend valuable time searching for answers, recreating existing materials, and navigating support processes.

This proposal recommends deploying a secure internal AI assistant that provides a single conversational entry point to approved organizational knowledge and selected workplace services. The assistant will help employees locate policies, summarize documents, draft content, and resolve common questions while respecting existing access permissions. It will support employees rather than replace professional judgment, with clear safeguards for sensitive information and consequential decisions.

## Objectives

The project’s primary objective is to reduce the time employees spend searching for information and performing repetitive knowledge-work tasks. The assistant will provide grounded answers with links to authoritative sources, improve access to internal guidance, and help employees produce first drafts and summaries more efficiently.

A second objective is to reduce avoidable demand on HR, IT, and other internal support teams by addressing common questions and directing employees to the correct services. The project will also establish a reusable foundation for future AI capabilities through standardized security controls, knowledge governance, evaluation practices, and integration patterns.

Deployment will prioritize measurable usefulness, trustworthy behavior, and sustainable operating costs. Success will be assessed through task outcomes and service improvements, not simply the number of conversations generated.

## Scope

The initial deployment will cover all 5,000 employees through a phased rollout, beginning with a representative pilot. Employees will access the assistant through an existing workplace collaboration platform or an authenticated web interface using organizational single sign-on.

The first release will support questions about approved HR policies, IT guidance, organizational procedures, and selected departmental knowledge. It will also offer document summarization, drafting assistance, and navigation to relevant forms and support channels. Responses based on internal knowledge will include source references, and the assistant will clearly indicate when information is unavailable or uncertain.

Integration will initially focus on a limited set of well-maintained repositories. Retrieval will enforce source-system permissions so that employees cannot obtain information they are not authorized to access. Confidential and restricted datasets will remain excluded until their use has been explicitly approved.

Autonomous changes to business systems, employment decisions, financial approvals, and unrestricted access to employee or customer records are outside the initial scope. Any later transactional capabilities will require a separate risk assessment, explicit authorization, appropriate human confirmation, and auditable controls.

## Timeline

The proposed delivery period is six months, subject to procurement readiness, integration complexity, and the quality of existing knowledge sources.

# Project Proposal: Enterprise AI Assistant Deployment

## Background

A 5,000-employee organization has a significant opportunity to improve how employees find information, produce routine work, and navigate internal processes. Knowledge is often distributed across document repositories, collaboration platforms, and business applications, requiring employees to search multiple systems or depend on colleagues for answers. An internal AI assistant can provide a single, conversational entry point to approved organizational knowledge and support common tasks such as drafting, summarizing, and explaining procedures.

This proposal recommends a phased, 24-week deployment that balances usefulness with security, reliability, and responsible adoption. The assistant will supplement employee judgment rather than replace it. Its responses will be grounded in authorized information where appropriate, identify supporting sources, and clearly communicate uncertainty. The rollout will begin with a representative pilot and expand only after defined quality, security, and operational readiness criteria are met.

## Objectives

The project’s primary objective is to reduce the time employees spend locating information and completing selected administrative and knowledge-work tasks. The assistant will help employees understand internal policies, locate relevant documents, summarize approved material, and prepare first drafts of routine communications and deliverables.

A second objective is to establish a secure, governed enterprise AI capability. Employees should be able to use AI through an approved service without exposing confidential information to unmanaged tools. The implementation will preserve existing access permissions, define acceptable uses, and provide clear accountability for platform operations and content quality.

The project will also build sustainable adoption through practical training, departmental champions, and continuous feedback. Success will be measured through demonstrated task improvements and response quality, not usage volume alone.

## Scope

The initial deployment will make the assistant available to all 5,000 employees through an enterprise web interface and, where supported, approved collaboration and mobile channels. Access will use organizational identity management, single sign-on, and role-based controls.

Initial capabilities will include question answering over approved internal knowledge, document summarization, drafting assistance, and guidance on routine IT, HR, and operational processes. Priority integrations will cover selected document repositories, the employee knowledge base, and service-desk content. Source owners will review material before onboarding so that outdated or conflicting information does not undermine response quality.

The assistant will retrieve only information the requesting employee is authorized to access. Controls will address encryption, retention, audit logging, sensitive-data handling, and attempts to manipulate the assistant through retrieved content. Vendor agreements must meet organizational requirements for data residency and prohibit the use of organizational data to train shared models.

The first release will not autonomously make employment decisions, approve payments, modify production systems, or provide definitive legal, medical, or financial advice. Transactional capabilities and additional business-system integrations will require separate approval. Employees will remain responsible for reviewing generated work before relying on it or distributing it, particularly in consequential contexts.

## Timeline and Delivery Approach

The project will run for 24 weeks, followed by a 90-day stabilization and benefits-measurement period.

During weeks one through four, the team will confirm priority use cases, establish baseline task measurements, assess data readiness, and complete initial security, privacy, and procurement reviews. This phase will produce an approved implementation plan, operating model, and evaluation framework.

Weeks five through eight will focus on platform configuration and initial integrations. The team will implement identity controls, permission-aware retrieval, monitoring, support processes, and a test suite covering accuracy, access restrictions, and unsafe behavior.

During weeks nine through twelve, approximately 300 employees from a representative mix of departments, roles, and locations will participate in a pilot. Participants will receive role-specific training and test the assistant against real tasks. Pilot findings will inform improvements to content, configuration, usability, and guidance. Expansion will require approval from the project sponsor and designated security and operational owners.

Weeks thirteen through eighteen will expand access to approximately 1,500 employees. This stage will validate support capacity, performance under higher demand, and the effectiveness of onboarding. Departmental champions will help identify useful workflows and recurring problems.

Weeks nineteen through twenty-four will extend access to the full organization in managed waves. The project will conclude with an operational handover, documented ownership, and an approved improvement backlog. The subsequent stabilization period will assess sustained adoption, task-level benefits, service reliability, and ongoing operating costs.

## Resource Requirements

Delivery will require an executive sponsor and a cross-functional team representing IT, security, privacy, legal, HR, internal communications, and major business functions. The core delivery effort is expected to require approximately eight to ten full-time-equivalent staff during implementation, combining a project manager, solution architect, integration engineers, an AI evaluation specialist, a security and privacy lead, a knowledge-management lead, and change-management and support capacity. Departmental champions and content owners will contribute part-time.

Technical resources will include an enterprise AI platform, secure hosting or an approved managed service, knowledge-retrieval infrastructure, identity integration, monitoring, and separate testing and production environments. Procurement will evaluate vendors on security, integration capability, response quality, accessibility, service commitments, and total cost.

For planning purposes, the first-year budget should allow approximately $2 million to $3.5 million for licensing or usage charges, implementation, staffing allocations, training, and support. This is an indicative range, not a vendor quotation. The budget will be refined during discovery using expected usage, licensing options, existing infrastructure, and internal staffing availability. Funding approval should distinguish implementation costs from recurring operating expenses and include contingency for integration or data-remediation work.

## Governance and Operational Readiness

A steering group will oversee scope, funding, risk acceptance, and rollout decisions. An accountable service owner will manage ongoing performance, vendor relationships, incidents, and the improvement roadmap. Content owners will remain responsible for the accuracy and currency of their source material.

Employees will receive clear guidance on permitted data, appropriate reliance on outputs, and how to report inaccurate or inappropriate responses. Material changes to models, integrations, or retrieval settings will undergo testing before release. High-risk findings will trigger remediation or suspension of the affected capability.

## Success Criteria

The deployment will be considered successful when all 5,000 employees have access to the approved service, at least 90% have completed the required onboarding, and at least 60% are monthly active users within 90 days of full rollout.

Quality will be assessed through a representative, independently reviewed test set. At least 90% of evaluated responses should correctly complete the intended task or appropriately acknowledge insufficient information. For answers requiring organizational evidence, at least 95% should provide valid supporting citations. All defined permission-boundary tests must pass, and no unresolved critical security findings may remain at a rollout gate.

Business value will be demonstrated through a target reduction of at least 15% in completion time for selected, repeatable tasks compared with discovery-phase baselines, without reducing output quality. This result will be measured through structured task comparisons rather than extrapolated into an unsupported organization-wide productivity claim.

Operational success will include 99.9% monthly availability during stabilization, responsive support, and an average user satisfaction rating of at least four out of five. Together, these measures will establish whether the assistant is useful, trustworthy, and sustainable enough to support broader capabilities in subsequent phases.

Workflow execution may be considered in a later phase, subject to separate approval and explicit confirmation controls.

It excludes organization-wide document remediation, replacement of existing business systems, and development of bespoke departmental agents beyond the agreed pilot use cases.

The team will measure task completion time, answer usefulness, citation accuracy, and support demand, while resolving quality or security issues.

During weeks thirteen through eighteen, access will expand to approximately 1,000 employees. This phase will validate performance under greater load, improve onboarding, and test the operating model across a broader range of roles. Additional content sources will be introduced only when ownership and permissions are verified.

The team will implement identity controls, connect the initial knowledge sources, prepare usage guidance, and create a test set covering representative questions and foreseeable failure cases. During weeks 9–12, approximately 200 employees will participate in a controlled pilot. Participants will represent different departments, roles, locations, and levels of technical confidence. The team will assess task completion time, answer quality, access-control behavior, usability, and support demand. An executive sponsor will be accountable for organizational alignment and funding. # Project Proposal: Organization-Wide Deployment of an Internal AI Assistant

## Background

A 5,000-employee organization generates substantial knowledge across documents, policies, project records, and internal communications. Yet employees often spend valuable time locating information, interpreting guidance, drafting routine materials, and navigating fragmented systems. An internal AI assistant can reduce this friction by providing a single, accessible interface for finding approved information and completing common knowledge-work tasks.

This proposal recommends a phased, six-month deployment of an internal AI assistant, supported by enterprise security controls, permission-aware access to internal content, and a structured adoption program. The assistant will augment employee judgment rather than replace it. Its value will be demonstrated through measured improvements in task completion, information quality, and employee experience before access expands across the organization.

## Objectives

The project will make organizational knowledge easier to find and use, reduce time spent on repetitive administrative work, and improve the consistency of routine communications and guidance. Initial capabilities will include answering questions about approved policies and procedures, summarizing authorized documents, drafting internal content, and helping employees prepare for meetings and projects.

A second objective is to establish a trusted operating model for AI. Employees should understand what the assistant can do, where its limitations lie, and when its output requires verification or specialist review. The deployment will therefore combine technical implementation with training, clear usage policies, and ongoing quality evaluation.

The project will also create a reusable foundation for future AI capabilities. Standardized integration patterns, governance processes, and evaluation methods will allow the organization to add approved use cases without rebuilding its security and operational controls.

## Scope

The deployment will provide access for all 5,000 employees through an enterprise-approved interface integrated with the organization’s identity provider and, where practical, its existing collaboration environment. Access will follow established roles and document permissions. The assistant must not reveal information that an employee could not otherwise access.

The initial knowledge base will prioritize high-value, well-maintained sources, including employee policies, IT support guidance, operating procedures, and selected departmental reference materials. Each source will have an identified owner responsible for accuracy, access permissions, and review cycles. Answers based on organizational knowledge will include source references wherever available, and the assistant will be expected to acknowledge when reliable information is missing.

The first release will support information retrieval, summarization, drafting, and recommendations. It will not autonomously approve transactions, modify systems of record, make employment decisions, or issue final legal, financial, medical, or compliance advice. Any later introduction of action-taking capabilities will require separate approval, narrowly defined permissions, and additional testing.

Security and privacy controls will include single sign-on, role-based access, encryption, appropriate audit logging, retention limits, and contractual restrictions on using organizational data to train shared models. Sensitive repositories will remain excluded until their inclusion is explicitly approved. Employee usage reporting will focus on aggregate adoption and service improvement rather than individual performance monitoring.

Governance will be shared across IT, security, privacy, legal, HR, and participating business functions. An executive sponsor and steering committee will approve scope changes, review risks, and authorize progression between rollout stages. Employees will have a clear mechanism for reporting incorrect answers, inappropriate content, and suspected data exposure.

## Timeline

The project will run over 24 weeks, with expansion dependent on meeting readiness criteria rather than calendar milestones alone.

During weeks one through four, the team will confirm priority use cases, assess platform options, establish baseline performance measures, and complete initial security, privacy, and procurement reviews. This phase will also identify content owners, select pilot participants, and define the evaluation framework and acceptable-use policy.

During weeks five through eight, the team will configure the platform, integrate identity and approved knowledge sources, and implement monitoring and support processes. Testing will address answer quality, source accuracy, access restrictions, malicious instructions embedded in retrieved content, and service reliability. Training materials and employee communications will be prepared before the pilot begins.

During weeks nine through twelve, approximately 250 employees representing different functions, locations, and working patterns will participate in a controlled pilot. The team will evaluate real-world usefulness, collect feedback, and compare selected tasks with established baselines. Material security or quality issues will be resolved before further deployment.

During weeks thirteen through eighteen, access will expand to approximately 1,250 employees in total. This stage will test operational capacity, refine onboarding, and validate whether pilot benefits persist across a broader population. Departmental champions will support adoption, while the project team will improve content coverage and address recurring failure patterns.

During weeks nineteen through twenty-four, the assistant will be rolled out to the remaining employees, subject to steering committee approval. The project will conclude with an operational handover, a benefits assessment, and a prioritized improvement roadmap. Adoption and business outcomes will continue to be measured during the first 90 days after organization-wide availability.

## Resource Requirements

Delivery will require a cross-functional team equivalent to approximately eight to ten full-time employees during implementation. Core capabilities will include project management, solution architecture, application and integration engineering, knowledge management, security and privacy review, quality evaluation, change management, and employee training. Some specialist responsibilities may be fulfilled through part-time contributions from existing teams.

Business functions will nominate content owners and departmental champions. Their participation is essential to ensure that information remains current, use cases reflect actual work, and employees receive relevant support. Following deployment, an ongoing team equivalent to three to five full-time employees will manage platform operations, integrations, content quality, evaluations, and adoption, with continued access to security and legal specialists.

The proposed first-year planning budget is $2.3 million to $3.4 million. This includes approximately $1.2 million to $1.8 million for platform licensing and model usage, $800,000 to $1.2 million for implementation and operational staffing, and $300,000 to $400,000 for infrastructure, security validation, training, and contingency. These figures are planning allowances rather than vendor quotations and assume organization-wide availability. Final funding will depend on procurement outcomes, existing technology entitlements, integration complexity, and expected usage.

## Success Criteria

The deployment will be considered successful if it delivers measurable employee value while meeting agreed security, quality, and operational standards.

Within 90 days of organization-wide availability, at least 90% of employees should have completed introductory training, and at least 60% should be weekly active users. Employee feedback should indicate that at least 80% of surveyed users find the assistant useful for one or more approved work activities.

For selected high-volume workflows, the project will target a minimum 15% reduction in task completion time without a decline in output quality. Results will be assessed against pre-deployment baselines using comparable tasks and, where feasible, matched user groups. Reported time savings will be distinguished from demonstrated financial savings or additional productive capacity.

Before each rollout expansion, the assistant must achieve at least 90% correctness on an approved, representative knowledge-question test set and at least 95% valid source support for answers requiring citations. All defined access-control tests must pass. No unresolved critical security or privacy defects may remain at a release gate, and any confirmed unauthorized disclosure during operation will trigger incident response and, where necessary, suspension of the affected capability.

Operational success will include meeting an agreed service-availability target of at least 99.5% during supported hours, maintaining responsive employee support, and assigning ownership and review schedules to every connected knowledge source. The final benefits review will recommend continued investment, targeted improvements, or scope reduction based on observed results.

By combining phased deployment, permission-aware knowledge access, employee enablement, and measurable release gates, this project will establish an internal AI service that can improve everyday work while preserving organizational accountability.

None of these is a major problem on its own, which is how you end up with forty-seven minor problems and one person who knows where the adapters are.

The useful plan is the one that gives those cases somewhere to go. Not a comments column that becomes a diary of unanswered emails, but an owner, a next action, and a date when somebody has to make a decision. Otherwise the old machines stay under desks, still connected, still technically awaiting collection. You discover them next year when you’re trying to work out why the support contract covers more devices than anyone remembers buying. By then the refresh has been marked complete for months.

Someone in finance has a macro that only runs on a version of Excel nobody admits is still installed. A field engineer needs a port that disappeared from the approved model three generations ago. There are fourteen laptops in a cupboard that count as available stock until you discover that eleven have no chargers and the other three belong to a project that ended in 2022. Each case is small enough to sound unreasonable when you raise it in a meeting. Together, they are where the schedule goes.

The useful question is not whether you can eliminate these exceptions. You cannot, and trying will mostly produce people who stop telling you about them. The useful question is who gets to make a decision when one turns up. Give that person a budget, a deadline, and permission to disappoint somebody. Otherwise every odd docking station becomes a policy discussion, every delayed migration becomes a personal favour, and the old machine stays under the desk because nobody wants to be responsible for the Tuesday it finally stops working.

One comes from the finance director, whose laptop apparently contains the only working copy of a macro that closes the books. Another comes from a warehouse where the label printer requires a driver last updated during the previous administration. Someone is on leave. Someone is in another country. Someone has received the replacement, put it under their desk, and continued using the old machine because nobody explicitly said not to. These are not edge cases to the people involved. They are Tuesday.

By this point the project plan has acquired a second life as a collection of notes in the margins. You are no longer replacing four hundred endpoints. You are negotiating four hundred small changes to how people get through their day, most of which were never documented because they worked well enough not to attract attention. The useful question stops being whether the new machines have arrived and starts being whether anyone can safely take the old ones away. That question tends to produce a less impressive status report, but a much more accurate one.

One laptop is running a finance tool that nobody has the installer for. Another belongs to someone who is technically on leave but still approves payroll. There are twelve machines in a regional office that were never in the inventory, and one executive who has interpreted “replacement” as “a second laptop.” None of these is a large problem on its own. That is what makes them so effective. Each one needs a small accommodation, a brief meeting, a temporary workaround. By week nine, the temporary workarounds have their own spreadsheet.

This is usually when somebody suggests tightening the process, which is a reasonable idea about three months too late. What you need now is less impressive: a name next to every exception, a date when it stops being an exception, and someone willing to ask whether the old machine has actually been returned. The new devices will arrive. They will mostly work. The difficult part is persuading the organization that a refresh cycle ends, rather than becoming another permanent layer of equipment, permissions, and things everyone agrees to sort out after the quarter closes.
